verdicts.trueWording: missed nuance, context and reading between the lines
verdicts.note: Appendix C (printed p.32), theme row 'Could not pick up nuance / context'; quote appears word for word. Appendix C is headed 'qualitative analysis of the debrief session and assessment rubric comments' and s.5.1 says such quotes are ASIC assessors' - the appendix does not label this individual quote debrief-vs-rubric. Raw PDF fetched and text-extracted; document is ASIC's answer to QoN No.001, Select Committee on Adopting AI.

verdicts.trueWording: a deep understanding of context, subtle nuances, or implicit meaning
verdicts.note: Section 6 Discussion, printed p.18 (PDF page 20), verbatim; the sentence begins 'Another significant issue was the LLMs limited ability to analyse and summarise complex content requiring ...' and continues that this led to summaries missing deeper implications. Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Included analysis which did not come from the document
verdicts.note: Section 5.1 Key Themes, printed p.17 (PDF page 19), under bullet 'Included incorrect information in summaries', prompt 'References to ASIC', attributed in the report to '(ASIC assessor)'; the same words recur in Appendix C. Verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: grammatically correct, but on occasion factually inaccurate
verdicts.note: Section 6.1 Limitations of the PoC, printed p.19, bullet 'Risk of hallucinations'; quote verbatim across a line break. The defining sentence is phrased generically ('Text-based Gen AI can on occasion generate texts that suffer from hallucinations, which means ...'), but the bullet is the PoC's own risk item and the report elsewhere records observed hallucination (Appendix, Model B, wage price spiral).

verdicts.trueWording: Asking the same question twice may not yield the same answer
verdicts.note: Section 6.1 Limitations, printed p.19, bullet 'Variation in outputs'; preceding sentence reads 'Testing was difficult due to low repeatability of model outputs.' Quote verbatim; every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: 51% of all AI answers to questions about the news
verdicts.note: BBC PDF fetched raw; executive-summary bullet on p.2 completes '... were judged to have significant issues of some form.' High-level findings repeats it as flagged 'by reviewers', and the methodology section says BBC journalists rated each response. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: 19% of AI answers which cited BBC content introduced factual errors
verdicts.note: Executive-summary bullet, p.2, continues '- incorrect factual statements, numbers and dates.' Verbatim; the 'such as' list matches exactly.

verdicts.trueWording: 13% of the quotes sourced from BBC articles were either altered
verdicts.note: Executive-summary bullet, p.2, continues 'from the original source or not present in the article cited.' Verbatim; both disjuncts of the claim supported.

verdicts.trueWording: 45% of responses contained at least one significant issue
verdicts.note: EBU PDF fetched raw; Foreword p.3 ('What have we found?', second point) reads 'Overall, 45% of responses contained at least one significant issue of any type.' High-level findings p.9 repeats it for all AI responses. Multi-market BBC-EBU study confirmed on the title page.

verdicts.trueWording: Sourcing is the single biggest cause of significant issues (31%)
verdicts.note: Foreword p.3, verbatim. Detailed figure on p.10: 'Sourcing was the biggest cause of problems, with 31% of all responses having significant issues with sourcing', so the 'of all responses' limb is supported too.

Quote is verbatim on p.10 of the EBU report, but the sentence reads 'were the next biggest contributors to significant issues' and Appendix 3 (results table) defines both figures as the share of ALL AI responses carrying that significant issue (accuracy 20%, context 14%) - not a breakdown of the significant issues themselves. Since 45% of responses had any significant issue, 20% of responses is roughly 44% of the issue-bearing responses, so the claim's denominator is wrong.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the '20 percent / 14 percent OF significant issues' denominator - the report gives these as percentages of all AI responses

verdicts.note: arXiv PDF fetched raw; Section 1 Introduction, p.6: 'when asked a direct, verifiable question about a randomly selected federal court case, LLMs hallucinate between 58% ... and 88% ... of the time.' Section 4 confirms the random sample spans USDC, USCOA and SCOTUS. All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: often uncritically accept users' incorrect legal assumptions
verdicts.note: Abstract, p.2 (curly apostrophe in the original); the sentence lists this alongside hallucinating at least 58% of the time. Section 5 develops it as contra-factual bias. All limbs supported.

arXiv PDF fetched raw; Table 3 row 'GPT-4o' gives Correct = 38.2. Abstract describes SimpleQA as evaluating models on 'short, fact-seeking questions'. One locator correction: Table 3 sits on printed page 7 of the arXiv v1 PDF (the caption follows the p.6 footer), not p.6 as cited.

Table 3 row 'OpenAI o1-preview' gives Correct = 42.7, the highest Correct score among the eight models listed (next: GPT-4o 38.2, Claude-3.5-sonnet 28.9); the text notes o1-preview outperforms o1-mini. Same locator correction as 1258: Table 3 is on printed p.7.
